JOHN BURROW'S SUPPLEMENTAL BRIEF ON
PRELIMINARY ORDER ISSUES NOS. 11 AND 13
TABLE OF CONTENTS

II. Issue No. 11 — Reliability Necessity	4
A. Regional Need and This Project	4
B. Gurley Testimony on the Combined Studies	6
C. December 2024 Sequencing Evidence	7

F. Power Available at Bell County East	10
III. Issue No. 13 — Consumer Congestion-Cost Savings	11
A. What congestion costs mean	13
B. What the statewide figures show	13

TO THE HONORABLE ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGES:
John Burrow, Bell County resident, graduate of Texas A&M University with a Bachelor of Science in Engineering, small business owner, not a lawyer, pro se intervenor, respectfully submits this Supplemental Brief addressing Preliminary Order Issues Nos. 11 and 13 pursuant to the Commission's remand and SOAH's orders. This brief relies on the existing evidentiary record and does not ask the ALJs to reopen that record.
I. INTRODUCTION AND SUMMARY
I am a landowner and a pro se intervenor in this case. I have extensive engineering experience in major construction projects in planning, funding, and execution of such projects.  I am not a lawyer, and I do not pretend to be one. But after months of reading studies, listening to and reading testimony, writing and reading motions and appeals, attending Senate and House hearings, attending Public Utility Commission meetings, and participating in the hearing for this case, the central problem is not complicated.  The Applicants have not proved a need for Import Path 2.  They did not prove that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards.
This matters. Preliminary Order Issue No. 11 does not ask whether Import Path 2 would be useful, beneficial, stronger than the existing system, or part of ERCOT's preferred long range plan. It asks whether the proposed transmission facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. The record shows the Applicants failed and their own statements prove they were not qualified or equipped to answer these questions for Import Path 2. 
I am an intervenor in Docket 59475, Bell County East to Big Hill. That is one part of Import Path 2. The other part, Docket 59182, is Big Hill to Sand Lake. While I am not an intervenor specifically in Docket 59182, based on the ALJ’s original PFD decision on need, my brief discusses and defends the need for the facilities in Dockets 59475 and 59182 that together comprise Import Path 2. 
The simplest way to understand the problem is this.  ERCOT put Import Paths 1, 2, & 3 into the system they modeled, and then the Applicants point to the performance of that system as proof that Import Path 2 is needed. But showing that a system works with a project in it is not the same as showing that the system fails without that project.
“System performance with Import Path 2 included is not proof of failure without Import Path 2 included.”
A simple bridge analogy makes the point. Imagine studying a highway system after three new bridges have already been built and then claiming the study proves that Bridge No. 2 had to be built. The study may prove the highway system works with all three bridges. It does not prove the system would fail without Bridge No. 2. To prove that, someone has to analyze what happens when Bridge No. 2 is not there. That is the missing analysis here.
The Applicants' own witness, Jared Gurley, admitted that he was not aware of a study that isolated each import path independently because the paths were studied together. The original PFD recognized exactly this problem and found that the Applicants did not establish the need for Import Path 2 separate from Import Paths 1 and 3.
Nothing identified fixes that problem. The later Regional Transmission Plans (RTP) assumed the 765-kV STEP in the planning cases. The Far West GTC exit strategy identifies the three Permian Basin 765-kV import paths collectively as part of a larger combination of projects. The economic numbers Applicants rely upon compare the statewide 765-kV STEP to a statewide 345-kV plan and the economic base cases; they do not tell the ALJs what congestion cost savings are attributed to Import Path 2 alone.
The ALJs got the central need question right the first time. I respectfully ask the ALJs to follow the evidence in this record, retain the original findings on need, and continue to recommend denial of the Application.
I am asking the ALJs to look at what the Applicants actually proved. We need to build what is needed and account for what we spend. The Applicants must show why this transmission line is needed.
II. ISSUE NO. 11: APPLICANTS DID NOT PROVE THAT IMPORT PATH 2 IS NECESSARY TO MEET A RELIABILITY STANDARD
Preliminary Order Issue 11. “Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards?” 
That is the question before the ALJs on remand. It does not ask whether Import Path 2 is useful, beneficial, or part of a larger ERCOT or Transmission Service Provider plan. It asks whether Import Path 2 is necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard.
A. A regional reliability problem is not proof that Import Path 2 is necessary or required.
There is no serious dispute that the Permian Basin region “may” have transmission constraints and reliability concerns. But proving that the Permian Basin region needs additional transmission from across Texas does not automatically prove that every project in a larger collection of transmission projects is independently necessary or required.
Applicants' own initial post hearing brief said that this Project, "in conjunction with the other Permian Basin Reliability Plan projects," would resolve reliability criteria violations under NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT planning criteria. This wording matters. It describes the performance of a group of transmission projects. It does not identify the specific reliability violation that exists because Import Path 2 is not included in that group or show that Import Path 2 is the project necessary to correct a violation. 
Applicants stated: "Yes. As described above, this Project, in conjunction with the other Permian Basin Reliability Plan projects, will resolve reliability criteria violations under NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1 and ERCOT planning criteria." 
Gurley’s direct testimony also identifies the 345-kV, 500-kV, and 765-kV import path alternatives as meeting NERC and ERCOT reliability criteria. ERCOT identified advantages for the 765-kV alternative, including greater transfer capability, fewer import paths, and less right-of-way. Those advantages may support ERCOT’s choice. But meeting reliability criteria does not, by itself, establish that this particular 765-kV configuration is the only compliant solution or answer whether Import Path 2 is necessary.
For Issue No. 11, the question should be straightforward. What specific reliability criterion fails if the other planned transmission facilities are built but Import Path 2 is not, and where in this record is the analysis showing that adding Import Path 2 fixes that failure? Applicants have not identified that analysis.
The Applicants' direct statements that Import Path 2 resolves reliability criteria violations lack credibility. They did not perform the PBRP study. They did not develop the PBRP cases. They state that they do not have the underlying demand and generation data beyond the published PBRP.  When asked for model information, they adamantly answer that they do not have it because ERCOT performed the studies.  They cannot accurately, specifically, and directly make statements that Import Path 2, alone, is necessary to resolve or fix reliability violations.
The central question for the Commission and ALJs is “What engineering analysis in this record establishes that a specific state or federal reliability criterion would fail without Import Path 2 and that adding Import Path 2 is necessary to fix that failure?” The answer is simple: “none.”
B. Applicants' own expert witness admitted the import paths were studied together.
Mr. Gurley's cross examination is one of the clearest pieces of evidence in this record. He testified that he was not aware of a study that isolated each line independently because "they were studied together." He then explained his view by referring to N-1 and N-1-1 requirements, but he did not identify a study that separately demonstrated the necessity of Import Path 2. 
Mr. Gurley testified: "I am not aware that, aware of a study that isolated each line independently as they were, they were studied together. In my belief, that's partially due to the requirements under TPL-001, the NERC requirement for this, that requires [N-1] and [N-1-1] studies. So you have to be able to remove an element during this study. So I assume, you know, that that leads into part of the recommendation for multiple lines." 
The Applicants argue that no law or NERC standard requires a study formally called a "partial-build study."  I am not asking the ALJs to create a new study requirement. The point is much simpler. Applicants must prove what the Commission asked them to prove. The Commission's certification rule requires a finding of necessity before a CCN may be granted. Whatever engineering method is used, it must establish that Import Path 2 is necessary to meet the applicable reliability standard.
The Applicants change the scope of their argument when it suits them. They argue Import Path 2 by itself when that supports their position. Then, when asked to prove its need or consumer savings, they argue all three Import Paths together. They cannot have it both ways. If they say the paths must be studied together, they still have to explain what those studies prove about the line they are asking to build in this case.
Oncor took a narrower position when it opposed Tom Green’s intervention in Docket 59029. In its appeal of SOAH Order No. 12, Oncor argued that the need issues were limited to the specific facilities in that case and that the same need issues would be “fully and independently addressed” for Dinosaur – Longshore, Big Hill – Sand Lake, and Bell County East – Big Hill, each in its own CCN docket. That position matters here. If need is to be addressed in each docket, Applicants still have to explain what the combined studies establish about the facilities they seek to build in this case.
The Commission’s April 8, 2026 order did not adopt a blanket rule that all three import paths are independent or stand-alone. It denied Tom Green’s intervention because he had not shown a legal right or justiciable interest in either Import Path 1 proceeding. But it upheld ABB Ranches’ intervention because the two Import Path 1 segments connect end to end and share common CCN issues. I am not claiming that this intervention ruling decides the engineering need for Import Path 2. I am asking Applicants to reconcile their position that need would be addressed separately in each CCN docket with their reliance here on studies of the paths together.
I understand that Import Path 2 is part of an interconnected electrical grid. I am asking what the evidence shows about this line. Showing that the whole plan works does not, by itself, show why Import Path 2 is necessary. Showing statewide cost savings does not tell us how much this line saves consumers. It is Applicants' job to prove their case. The other parties that were forced to enter the combatant ring should not have to disprove the whole plan every time Applicants change the scope of their argument.
The question on remand is whether Applicants proved that these proposed facilities are necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. Applicants must answer that question with evidence about this line. Saying the whole plan is beneficial does not, by itself, answer it. Issue No. 13 also asks what congestion cost savings consumers may receive from these proposed facilities. Statewide savings figures do not answer that question unless Applicants explain how those savings are connected to this line. I ask the ALJs to answer both questions from the admitted evidence and retain the original findings on need.
An N-1 or N-1-1 contingency analysis performed on a system that already contains Import Path 2 answers a different question. It does not show whether Import Path 2 had to be built in the first place.
C. ERCOT's December 2024 sequencing letter/evidence makes the missing proof more important.
ERCOT's December 12, 2024, sequencing letter/evidence stated that two of the three 765-kV import paths were needed by 2030. On cross examination, Mr. Martin acknowledged the words on the page say that two of the three import paths are needed. The letter does not, by itself, identify which 765-kV path was the third path, but the PFD considered the sequencing evidence together with the rest of the record when evaluating whether Import Path 2 had been shown to be independently necessary by 2030. 
ERCOT letter stated: "Two of the four 345-kV import paths and two of the three 765-kV import paths are needed by 2030."  
When asked directly whether the letter says only two of the three are needed, Mr. Martin answered: "The words on the page say that two of the three are needed." 
The Applicants say later studies show all three paths are needed by 2030. If that is their position, there should be a clear bridge in the evidence between those two conclusions. What changed? Which reliability violation made the third path necessary? Which analysis shows that the system fails without Import Path 2? The record identified by the Applicants does not provide a project specific answer to those questions.
Putting all three import paths into later planning cases and then relying on those cases does not supply the missing bridge. Once Import Path 2 is assumed in the starting topology, the study can tell us how the system performs with Import Path 2. It cannot, by that fact alone, tell us what happens without it.
The evidence shows the sequencing letter did indicate two of the three paths were needed by 2030 and that it does not say which path was the third. In addition, Gurley's rebuttal says the sequencing spreadsheet showed the reliability need for all three paths beginning to appear in 2038. He also points to the later RTP's 2030 core plan. Applicants should explain what changed and why that change shows Import Path 2 is needed.
D. The 2024 and 2025 RTPs do not independently prove Import Path 2.
The timing and purpose of these materials should be kept clear. The Application’s need discussion relied on the PBRP study. The 2024 RTP comparison was included with Gurley’s direct testimony filed on the same day as the Application; it was not the original PBRP need study. The fuller 2024 RTP and the 2025 RTP were introduced later with Gurley’s rebuttal testimony. Their later introduction does not prevent the ALJs from considering them to the extent they were admitted. My point concerns what that evidence proves about these proposed facilities, not whether admitted evidence can be considered because it came later.
Applicants rely heavily on the later RTPs. But their own evidence says the 2025 RTP included all three 765-kV import paths in the 2030 and 2031 study cases, and Applicants have argued that later planning models assumed the 765-kV import paths would be in service by 2030. That matters because a study that starts with Import Path 2 already in the model can show how that modeled system performs; it does not, alone, show which state or federal criteria would be violated without Import Path 2. 
This is not an insignificant detail. It means later planning was performed on a system that already assumed the Import Paths were in service. Continued use of an assumption is not the same thing as independently proving the assumption. Assumption is not necessity.
I am not asking the ALJs to reject ERCOT planning and I realize the authority to audit resides with the Commission. I am asking the ALJs to answer the question presented in this CCN: whether the evidence proves that Import Path 2 itself is necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard. 
Applicants will point to the 2030 core plan and ERCOT's test with lower projected loads. The 2024 RTP says key reliability needs remained similar when officer letter loads were reduced from more than 31 GW to less than 16 GW. ERCOT tested the 2026 and 2029 summer peak cases and the 2027 minimum load case. That supports the broader plan. But the starting case for the 765-kV comparison already included all three Permian import paths. The test does not, by itself, show why Bell County East to Big Hill or Import Path 2 as a whole is necessary.
The 2025 RTP says STEP continued to help serve new load growth and ERCOT saw no need to change or remove any part of it. That supports the Applicants' argument. But the same passage says the whole STEP was already included in the 2030 and 2031 starting cases. Gurley also testified that he knew of no study testing each line separately. Saying the whole plan still helps does not, by itself, show why Import Path 2 is necessary.
E. The Far West GTC evidence treats the three 765-kV import paths as a single project.
The Applicants point to the Far West Import GTCs as their strongest later evidence. Those constraints are serious. The PFD already examined this evidence and described the April 2026 ERCOT Far West GTC presentation more carefully.  The 765-kV import paths were "expected to help" exit the Far West Import GTCs by 2030. "Expected to help" is not the same thing as "independently necessary." 
Mr. Martin goes further and concludes that all three paths, including Import Path 2, are critical. On cross-examination, however, he acknowledged the GTC study was an ERCOT document and that Applicants did not run the power flows that produced the exit strategy. That does not make the ERCOT study invalid. It does mean the ALJs should look closely at what the study itself proves rather than simply adopting a broader conclusion placed on it by the Applicants.
The question is not whether the entire package of projects helps retire the GTCs. The question is whether this record shows the GTCs cannot be retired with the other identified exit projects within the Permian Basin and the other 765-kV import paths but without Import Path 2. The collective label "Permian Basin 765 kV Import Paths" does not itself answer that project-specific question.
The April 2, 2026 presentation tests difficult grid conditions. It includes four Far West Texas Energy Fund generators that met Planning Guide § 6.9(1), along with large loads supported by interconnection agreements and officer letters. It assumes no real power output from solar or batteries and tests wind output at 15% and 10%. It studies several transmission improvements together. The slides do not show a separate test without Bell County East to Big Hill or Big Hill to Sand Lake or without Import Path 2 as a whole or estimate how much this line alone saves consumers. I am not saying the other transmission facilities would be enough. I am asking what this study proves about Import Path 2.
F. The Bell County East problem remains.
The original PFD also identified a problem at the eastern end of Import Path 2. The ALJs found that the Applicants did not prove sufficient power would be available at Bell County East for a westward transfer of power, did not quantify Central Texas net generation, and did not perform a study addressing whether Central Texas generation could serve its own growing load and at the same time support a west transfer of power. 
That is not a technical side issue. If the claimed purpose of Import Path 2 is to move large amounts of power west through Bell County East, it is reasonable to ask whether the modeled system can deliver the assumed power to Bell County East while also serving Central Texas. The PFD found that the Applicants did not make that showing. The remand does not change that.   
The Applicants may say the grid is interconnected and the power does not have to come from Bell County. But that’s not what the application says. The question is, can enough power be generated or reach Bell County East and move west while the system still serves its other loads? The PFD found that Central Texas also needs imported power and that questions about generation and load had not been answered. My concern is whether the power can get there.
III. ISSUE NO. 13: THE RECORD DOES NOT QUANTIFY CONGESTION COST SAVINGS ATTRIBUTED TO IMPORT PATH 2
Preliminary Order Issue 13. "What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission facilities to reduce those congestion levels?" 
This wording matters. The question asks for savings that may result from "the proposed transmission facilities," not the economic performance of the statewide 765-kV combination of projects.  It is asking about savings, specifically the estimated congestion cost savings to consumers, that may result from the proposed Import Path 2 transmission facilities the Applicants want approved in this application.
The important words are "the proposed transmission facilities." The proposed transmission facilities in Dockets 59475 and 59182 together comprise Import Path 2. 
The Applicants repeatedly characterized this application as a reliability project rather than an economic project. The PFD therefore found that the economic cost benefit test was not required for this reliability project and, importantly, that the record contained no evidence quantifying the consumer congestion cost savings for this application or Import Path 2.
The Applicants point to economic benefits from the 2024 RTP comparison. But those numbers compare a statewide base case to the statewide 765-kV STEP against a statewide 345-kV plan. They are a combination of statewide figures. They do not tell the ALJs how much congestion cost savings or consumer energy savings are attributable to this application or Import Path 2. 
There is another limit to what the economic comparison shows. The January comparison explains that its 2034 and 2039 economic base cases did not include the large loads supported by TSP officer letters because those loads were not available when the cases were developed. The economic cases therefore do not use the same demand assumptions as the reliability showing. The complete 345-kV and 765-kV plans were added separately to those economic base cases. That is a comparison of the plans, but it does not isolate Import Path 2. Applicants should explain how those economic results relate to the loads and timing used to support this project’s reliability need. The different assumptions do not make the economic study invalid or prove that savings are zero.
Mr. Martin made the limitation especially clear on cross-examination. Asked whether his rebuttal offered an opinion on the cost of Import Path 2, he confirmed that it did not. Asked whether he compared the cost of Import Path 2 against alternatives, he answered: "My testimony does not address cost." 
Q. "And your rebuttal testimony didn't offer any opinions on the cost of Import Path 2. Is that correct?" A. "(Martin) That's correct." Q. "And you didn't compare the cost of the Import Path 2 against any of the alternatives anywhere in your testimony, did you?" A. "(Martin) My testimony does not address cost." 
A comparison of a statewide portfolio of projects cannot simply be assigned to this project without evidence showing what portion of the savings is caused by this application or Import Path 2. The Application and the record cited by Applicants do not quantify congestion-cost savings attributable specifically to Import Path 2 or isolate a comparison between building and not building Import Path 2 while accounting for the other planned facilities. That missing connection is the problem; it does not establish that the savings are zero.
The problem is not whether the statewide economic numbers are accurate. Even assuming they are accurate, they answer a different question. Issue No. 13 asks for the estimated congestion cost savings resulting from this application or Import Path 2. The Applicants have provided statewide project numbers without showing what portion, if any, is attributable to this application or Import Path 2. A statewide total cannot answer a project specific question unless the record contains an analysis connecting that total to this project.
The same bridge analogy applies to Issue No. 13. If three bridges and several new highways are built, the total fuel and travel time savings from the entire transportation plan do not tell us the savings produced by Bridge No. 2. Unless the analysis separates Bridge No. 2 from the rest of the plan, no one can tell what savings Bridge No. 2 actually produced. The statewide 765-kV project numbers have the same problem here.
 From the Applicants’ exhibits on annual modeled amounts in 2025 dollars: 
A. What congestion costs mean
The table they show reports two different things: congestion rent and consumer energy cost. A reduction in congestion rent does not mean consumers save that same amount on their energy costs. For 2034, statewide congestion rent is $1.873 billion in the Base Case, $1.539 billion under the 345-kV plan, and $1.444 billion under the 765-kV plan. That is about $429 million less under the 765-kV plan than in the Base Case. Compared with the 345-kV plan, the rounded numbers show about $95 million less; ERCOT reports $94 million. These numbers cover the whole statewide plan. They do not show $429 million in savings on consumers' bills or tell us how much this application or Import Path 2 saves.
B. What the statewide figures show
Now look at the consumer energy cost column. For 2034, ERCOT reports $18.342 billion in the Base Case, $18.143 billion under the 345-kV plan, and $18.279 billion under the 765-kV plan. Using those rounded numbers, the 765-kV plan reduces modeled consumer energy cost by about $63 million compared with the Base Case. But its consumer energy cost is about $136 million higher than the 345-kV plan. That is why the $429 million reduction in congestion rent cannot simply be called $429 million in consumer savings. The two columns measure different costs.
The 2039 numbers appear better for the 765-kV plan. Compared with the statewide 345-kV plan, ERCOT reports about $229 million less in consumer energy cost and $172 million less in congestion rent. Applicants may rely on those results. I am not saying the 765-kV plan may never help consumers. The results depend on the year being studied. But neither year's statewide numbers tell us how much this application or Import Path 2 saves consumers.
C. What remains unproved for this application or Import Path 2
The Far West Import GTCs do not answer the dollar question either. A GTC limits how much power can move through the grid so it can operate reliably. Removing that limit may help, but it does not tell us how many dollars consumers save. The April presentation shows plans for removing the GTCs. It does not calculate consumer savings from this application or Import Path 2. The statewide economic comparison was published in January 2025, before the September 2025 import GTCs and the April 2026 presentation. Those earlier tables cannot, by themselves, tell us the savings from this application or Import Path 2 in removing those limits.
To estimate this line’s savings, Applicants need to show what difference the line makes. One way is to compare the system with and without these facilities, keeping the assumptions about load, generation, dispatch, and GTC limits consistent. Another reliable method could show the line’s contribution while accounting for the other projects. I am not asserting that the law requires a study with a particular name or format. I am asking whether the admitted evidence supplies the project-specific estimate requested in Issue No. 13. Past congestion and the ability to move more power may show why a line has value. They do not, by themselves, tell us how much money consumers save because of it.
I am not asking the ALJs to make up a number. I am asking them to say what the evidence shows. If savings have not been measured, that does not mean they are zero. And modeled consumer energy cost does not tell us the final change in a customer's bill after customers pay for the new transmission facilities. My point is simple: the statewide studies and GTC presentation cited here do not estimate the consumer congestion cost savings from the facilities in this application or Import Path 2.
Applicants may say a reliability project does not have to pass an economic cost-benefit test. PURA § 37.056(d) addresses projects that are not necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. The original PFD treated this as a reliability project and found that an economic analysis was not required. It also found that consumer costs and congestion savings had not been measured. I am not asking for a new economic test for every reliability project. I am asking for an answer to Issue No. 13. The burden of proof is with the Applicants, and they failed to prove what savings are attributable to the facilities in this application or Import Path 2.
ERCOT-wide savings and project-specific savings are not opposites. The economic-project provisions of 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(A)(i) measure savings across ERCOT, but require those savings to be attributable to the proposed project. The congestion test compares levelized annual congestion-cost savings with the average annual revenue requirement for the first three years; the production test compares levelized annual production-cost savings with the first-year annual revenue requirement. I recognize that those economic tests do not apply to a transmission line necessary to meet state or federal reliability standards. I am not asking the ALJs to impose those tests here. I am asking them to answer Issue No. 13. Applicants’ directory points to statewide STEP results and testimony about congestion relief, but does not identify a dollar estimate attributable to the facilities in this application or Import Path 2, or a project-specific revenue-requirement comparison. The record cited by Applicants therefore does not establish the congestion-cost savings from building these facilities rather than not building them. That is a missing estimate, not proof of zero savings or, by itself, failure of a legally required economic test.
IV. THE ALJS' ORIGINAL FINDINGS REMAIN SUPPORTED BY THE RECORD
After a full hearing, the ALJs found that Applicants did not prove sufficient power available at Bell County East for westward transfer; did not perform the relevant Central Texas generation studies; did not establish Import Path 2's need separate from the Import Paths 1 and 3; and did not establish that Import Path 2 was needed in 2030 for the forecasted Permian Basin load. 
The PFD stated that "the Commission must determine in this CCN case whether Import Path 2 is independently necessary." The PFD then noted the Applicants had not performed a partial build study to justify Import Path 2 individually and considered ERCOT's statement that only two of the three 765-kV import paths were needed by 2030. 
The remand asks the ALJs to address Issues Nos. 11 and 13. It does not erase the evidence that produced those findings. When Issue No. 11 evidence is examined directly, the same basic problem remains. The studies establish the need for substantial transmission and evaluate a combination of projects containing Import Path 2, but they do not isolate and prove the necessity of Import Path 2 itself.
The engineering may be complicated, but the ultimate question is not. The question can be understood in plain English. If the Applicants say Import Path 2 is necessary, the record should show what fails without it. That is missing.
V. THE APPLICANTS CANNOT USE ERCOT AS BOTH THEIR SWORD AND THEIR SHIELD.
The Applicants want the conclusion without owning the analysis. They tell the Commission and ALJs Import Path 2 will resolve NERC and ERCOT reliability violations. But when asked for the modeling foundation, their own answers are: ERCOT performed the study; ERCOT developed the cases; the Applicants do not have the underlying load and generation data; and the Applicants do not have other requested modeling information. That may establish that ERCOT recommended a combination of projects. It does not establish that this application or Import Path 2 itself is necessary or required to meet state or federal reliability standards. The Commission asked whether Import Path 2 is necessary, not whether a package of projects that includes Import Path 2 meets the standards. 
Applicants' September 21 directory lists evidence they rely on, including the core plan, the GTC exit strategy, and the economic tables. The ALJs should look at that evidence. A list of citations does not change what the studies prove.
Applicants will also say ERCOT's recommendation deserves great weight. The original PFD considered that argument. It found that even with great weight given to ERCOT's recommendation, the greater weight of credible evidence was against accepting it for Import Path 2. I ask the ALJs to keep that reasoning. They can respect ERCOT's expertise and still consider the problems they found in the evidence for this Project.
VI. PRAYER
I respectfully ask the Administrative Law Judges to use the same careful judgment and common sense they used in the original PFD, follow the evidence admitted in this case, retain the original findings concerning the failure to prove project need, and continue to recommend denial of the Application.
This case carries enormous consequences for landowners and ratepayers. A project of this size should not receive an approval based on assumptions, a 30-thousand-foot level conclusion, or the idea that opponents must disprove a project that the Applicants were required to justify. Before private property is confiscated and billions of dollars in transmission investment are placed on the ratepayers, the evidence should clearly establish the project is necessary. This record does not.
I know there is frustration and distrust surrounding this proceeding. Public officials, legislators, landowners, and ratepayers have raised serious concerns about the process, the modeling, the cost, the need for these projects, and the SOAH ALJs’ recommendation of denial of Import Path 1 being overruled by the PUC Commissioners. This limited remand should not be decided because of political pressure, accusations, or who has the loudest voice, or the most money. It should be decided on the admitted evidence. The record itself is enough. 
SOAH exists to provide an independent hearing and an evidence based recommendation. The ALJs heard the witnesses, reviewed the studies, considered the cross examination, and concluded that the Applicants did not prove the need for this application and Import Path 2. The Commission remanded Issues Nos. 11 and 13 for further consideration, but the limited remand does not supply the missing project specific proof. If the proof was not there after a full hearing, it should not be created by assumption now.
I ask the ALJs to explain in the supplemental PFD that these studies look at several projects together, the GTC evidence does not resolve the problems identified at PFD pages 82–89, and the economic tables do not show consumer congestion cost savings from Import Path 2 proposed facilities. Those findings would answer the remanded issues and support keeping the recommendation to deny the Application based on the admitted evidence.
I ask the ALJs to find that the Applicants have not established a quantified estimate of congestion cost savings attributable specifically to Import Path 2. The amount is unestablished.
I respectfully ask the ALJs to take the time necessary for a careful review of the admitted evidence and a fully supported answer to both remanded issues. We are no longer on a mandated 180-day death march.  We have the time and with families’ land and billions of dollars in ratepayer obligations at stake, the importance of getting this decision right warrants deliberate consideration. 
For those reasons, I respectfully ask the ALJs to stand by the evidence and common sense, retain their original findings on need, and recommend that the Commission DENY the Application.
